[0] everyday_reading (E): Folk meaning: in prose, indentation and line layout show what belongs to what, and two consecutive 'if' sentences can be heard as one combined condition. The Java compiler ignores indentation: an inner if belongs to the branch that syntactically contains it, and an else pairs with the innermost unmatched if.
[1] misconception (M) -> InnerIfIgnoresOuter: wrong rule: An inner if runs its body whenever its own condition is true, even if the outer if condition is false. Right rule: The inner if is part of the outer branch: it is reached, and its condition tested, only when the outer condition is true.
[2] misconception (M) -> SequentialIfsAreNested: wrong rule: Of two if statements one after the other, the second runs its body only if both conditions are true. Right rule: Two ifs in sequence are independent: each tests only its own condition.
[3] inconsistent_trace (T) -> InnerIfIgnoresOuter: Applies the nesting rule (LT) unevenly: on some inputs tests the inner condition even though the outer one was false, or matches an else to the if it is lined up with. (here mixing in: "An inner if runs its body whenever its own condition is true, even if the outer if condition is false")
[4] misconception (M) -> ElseMatchesIndentation: wrong rule: The else belongs to the if it is lined up with. Right rule: The else belongs to the most recent unmatched if, whatever the indentation.
[5] misconception (M) -> MultipleElseIfBranchesRun: wrong rule: Every true branch of an else-if chain runs. Right rule: Only the first branch whose condition is true runs.
[6] misconception (M) -> NestedIfsInsteadOfLogicalOperators: wrong rule: A condition on several values has to be written as nested if statements, one value per if. Right rule: Several conditions combine into one boolean expression with && and ||, e.g. if (x == 0 && y == 0).

[0] names_the_element (N): Nested conditionals are if or if-else statements placed inside a branch of another conditional; an else-if chain is the common special case.
[1] states_the_rule (S): An if/if-else is a statement, so it can be the body (branch) of another conditional; without braces an else belongs to the innermost if to which it might belong, so braces should be used to resolve ambiguities.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Test the outer condition; only if control enters the branch that contains the inner if is the inner condition tested; after the inner statement, control leaves the outer statement too.
[1] output_prediction (OP): The output is the action of the single path whose conditions all hold along the way: if (a > b) { if (b > c) X; else Y; } else Z; runs X when a > b > c, Y when a > b and b <= c, and Z otherwise.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): One execution evaluates the conditions along one path only (outer, then possibly inner) and applies one leaf action; conditions on other paths are never evaluated.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): Nesting puts an if or if-else inside a branch of another if-else; when the inner statement fills the else branch it forms an else-if chain.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): The dangling-else ambiguity arises when ifs are nested without braces: if <e1> if <e2> A else B attaches else to the inner if.
[2] relation_to_neighbour (R): For more than two mutually exclusive alternatives a chain of if-else statements works, but a switch tests one expression against many values directly.
[3] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Plan: decision tree - refine a case analysis step by step (e.g. find the smallest of three values, classify a value into ranges).

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> InnerIfIgnoresOuter: Combining if (c1) { if (c2) S; } into if (c1 && c2) S; preserves behaviour when there are no else parts; adding or removing braces around an inner if can move an else to a different if. Swapping some branches can keep the specification only on certain inputs.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Nest conditionals when a second test only makes sense once the first has succeeded or when cases form a tree; use && for a simple conjunction, an else-if chain for mutually exclusive ranges, and a switch for many discrete values; one or two levels usually suffice.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Without braces an else pairs with the innermost if, whatever the indentation. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: if (a) if (b) X; else Y; written with else under the outer if: Y runs when a is true and b false, not when a is false.

When there are more than two mutually exclusive alternatives, a chain of if-else statements works, but a switch statement provides a direct solution that evaluates one expression against many possible values.
Nesting puts an if or if-else inside a branch of another if-else; an else-if chain is the common case where the else branch is itself an if.
An if statement can sit inside the body of another if; the inner one is tested only when the outer condition is true.
The dangling else arises when ifs are nested without braces.
